claims.text: A precisely engineered tempering schedule can produce a reversible ductile–brittle–ductile transition in conventional martensitic steel.
Temper embrittlement in martensitic steel occurs in a narrow temperature range of approximately 350–450 °C.
Staged heating, isothermal holding, and controlled cooling through the embrittlement window can control the transition.
Time at temperature and rapid thermal ramping can be used to manage impurity-segregation dynamics.
Temporary grain-boundary segregation of impurities such as phosphorus or carbon transiently embrittles the steel.
The steel is ductile at temperatures below the proposed embrittlement window.
Entering the 350–450 °C range causes grain-boundary impurity segregation and brittle behavior.
Further thermal processing can alleviate impurity segregation or transform the precipitate distribution.
Alleviating segregation or transforming the precipitate distribution restores ductility.
The proposed treatment will yield ductile behavior initially, brittle behavior in the embrittlement window, and recovered ductility after additional treatment.
Conventionally processed tempered martensitic steel typically undergoes unwanted, irreversible embrittlement rather than a controlled reversible transition.
The proposed effect is limited to conventional alloy systems that exhibit temper embrittlement.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys may lack the proposed temper-embrittlement mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial material is simultaneously described as 'tempered' and 'as-quenched'; these normally denote different thermal states.
